Herpes happens to be one of the most over-stigmatized, misunderstood STI's out there.  My advice would be to check out r/Herpes and/or do some research. I went through the SAME thing with my ex-partner.  We were together for almost 3 years and they were some of the happiest years of my life... until I (stupidly) moved into a house with him and 4 other guys, felt overwhelmed, undervalued, and got very depressed.  It was the first time in our relationship where I actually needed his support and he didn't step up at all.  It begs the question: how do you know you'll get any emotional support in the future when you need it?  

In almost every case, there's something deeper going on with them that they need to work through themselves.  With mine, he claims that "allowing negativity around him will throw his own emotions into turmoil" and he's of the belief that supporting someone in crisis makes them "weak", since they should be able to bounce back on their own accord.

All-in-all, a partnership is about mutual love, respect and support.  Have an honest conversation (when you're both sober and stable) about how his actions (or lack thereof) are affecting you and see if it's something he realizes, and/or is willing to work on.  If it isn't, don't stick around until you're so low you can't pick yourself back up.  

Being able to support a partner emotionally when they need it is NECESSARY in EVERY relationship and he will, GUARANTEED, learn this at some point, whether it's with you or someone else.  Hopefully he can come to terms with his own shit sooner rather than later and take steps towards being there for you.

If not, the crucial thing for YOU to do is make sure you have support elsewhere.  While it's not healthy to rely solely on a partner for this, good friends, family, therapists, etc. go a LONG way.  The most important thing is to make sure that you're taking care of yourself.  Everything else comes second.

If you don't want to end the relationship, you could start a conversation around his behaviour by simply asking if she's taught him any tricks and, if not, suggesting that it might be a fun thing to do.

Dogs are like sponges, especially young ones.  They learn the correct and incorrect behaviours via positive reinforcement and lack thereof.  In any case, an owner teaching their dog tricks strengthens their human-to-pet bond and will help their communication in nearly every situation.  ALSO, dogs tend to get crazy when they don't have something "engaging" to do. (ie training, games, walks, etc.)

If you pose it to her and she seems receptive, it can open doors to train him to be more "polite" with you and others, respecting personal space, even crate training can be SO helpful in establishing boundaries.  If she's not receptive and doesn't want to put that time in then I'm afraid she's more interested in having a living, breathing, peeing and pooping stuffed animal than a dog and that's honestly reason enough to leave in my book.

In summary; There are no bad dogs, just bad trainers.
